questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Leading Entries of a Matrix
questions.problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 & 8 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st and $4$th rows of $A$ are $1$ and $-3$, respectively.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 & 8 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the answer is $1+(-3)=-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${a}_{43}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${c}_{32}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are **not** in row echelon form.

Which entries of $A$ could be replaced by $0$ in order to get a matrix in row echelon form?

$$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that by replacing ${a}_{21}$ and ${a}_{43}$ with $0$, we get a matrix in row echelon form:

$$

$$

The other options will not give us a matrix in row echelon form.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Operations That Would Transform a Matrix To Row Echelon Form
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ given below.
Which entries of $A$ could be replaced by $0$ in order to get a matrix in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 6 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that by replacing ${a}_{32},$ ${a}_{33},$ and ${a}_{41}$ with $0$, we get a matrix in row echelon form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 6 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,⟶\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The other options will not give us a matrix in row echelon form.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Leading Entries of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071571/assets/a29e80b35c9505ee665a109978de9b936ee7ce59eef631d7af9a4b7954bd8696.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows of $A$ are $-1$, $-4$ and $8$, respectively.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071571/assets/d2f89fe83787daf667e01fd4c4fe644bc36cfe23b046088c22e8de17bb02dc28.png)

So, the answer is $-1+(-4)+8=3.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071571/assets/e300a9ac18f0170ae9053c9635fe13a9dd6def793ebfc0bd9dbe81e28810a347.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14071571/assets/5d576fca72f6a4f9f0668ff0efbdc2cacc33f8dbb2c00192a7397da9ec83adea.png)

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.
